meta.title: Embeddings and Vector Search
meta.thesis: An embedding turns text into a point in space so that meaning becomes distance; vector search then answers 'what is closest in meaning?' — the retrieval engine behind semantic search and RAG.

modules.title: Mental model
modules.sub: Build the simplest useful picture of Embeddings and Vector Search.
modules.summary: Keyword search matches letters; embeddings match meaning. This module frames the whole topic: text becomes a point in space, and similarity becomes distance.
objectives: Explain what an embedding is in one plain sentence.
Say why keyword search fails on questions phrased differently from the source.
Picture text as points in a meaning-space where closeness equals similarity.

blocks.title: Why embeddings exist: the problem keyword search can't solve

spans.text: Imagine a help centre. A user types
"my card got declined"
, but the right article is titled
"payment failed at checkout"
. Keyword search shares no words, so it finds nothing — even though the meaning is identical.
That is the gap
embeddings
close. An
embedding
turns a piece of text into a list of numbers — a point in space — positioned so that texts with similar meaning sit close together, even when they share no words.
Before reading on, predict:
if "my card got declined" and "payment failed" become two points in space, what would you measure to decide they mean the same thing?

blocks.analogy: An embedding is like pinning every sentence onto a giant map: sentences about the same idea land in the same neighbourhood, no matter what words they used to get there.

blocks.title: The core idea: meaning becomes distance

spans.text: Hold three ideas together and the rest of this lesson follows.

items.text: model reads text and outputs a fixed-length list of numbers (often hundreds of them).
The model is trained so that related texts land close together and unrelated texts land far apart.
embeds your query and returns the points closest to it — the most similar texts.

spans.text: This is also the engine behind
RAG
: retrieve the most relevant passages by meaning, then hand them to a language model as evidence before it answers.

blocks.title: Meaning-space: pick a query, see its neighbours
blocks.caption: Each point is a short text placed by meaning. Pick a query and watch the nearest points light up — that is exactly what vector search returns.

blocks.title: Click through the flow
blocks.caption: The smallest useful sequence: text becomes vectors, a query finds the nearest ones.

steps.label: Text
steps.detail: A document or question enters as plain words.

steps.label: Embed
steps.detail: An embedding model turns it into a vector — a point in meaning-space.

steps.label: Compare
steps.detail: Vector search measures distance from the query point to every stored point.

steps.label: Return
steps.detail: The closest points come back as the most similar texts.

blocks.title: Concrete use case: the help-centre search box

spans.text: A support team has 500 help articles. With keyword search, "my card got declined" returns nothing useful because no article uses those exact words.
They switch to
vector search

. Each article is embedded once and stored. The query is embedded at search time, and the nearest article — "payment failed at checkout" — comes back first. Same meaning, different words, correct result.
That is the pattern to copy: embed the corpus once, embed each query, return nearest neighbours.

blocks.prompt: Why does keyword search miss the article "payment failed at checkout" when the user types "my card got declined"?

options.text: The article is too long to index.
Keyword search matches shared words, and these two phrases share none — even though they mean the same thing.
The user used too many words.

blocks.explanation: Keyword search compares literal tokens. Embeddings compare meaning, so semantically equivalent phrasings land near each other regardless of wording.

modules.title: Mechanism
modules.sub: Follows the mental model: open the pipeline that turns text into searchable points.
modules.summary: Now we open the box. Text is chunked, each chunk is embedded into a vector, vectors are stored in an index, and a query is embedded and matched by distance. Knowing each stage tells you where quality is won or lost.
objectives: Name the five stages of the retrieval pipeline in order.
Explain what a chunk is and why text is split before embedding.
Describe how similarity is measured between two vectors.

spans.text: Before reading on, predict from memory:
in module 1 you met the core idea. What does an
embedding
turn a piece of text into, and what does "close together" mean for two texts?
Answer it, then continue. (An embedding turns text into a vector — a point in meaning-space. Two texts close together mean similar things. This module shows the machinery that makes that happen.)

blocks.title: The retrieval pipeline, stage by stage

spans.text: Building a searchable corpus and answering a query is one pipeline with two phases. Indexing happens once; querying happens on every request.

items.text: Load the raw documents you want to search.
Split each document into smaller passages —
— because one vector cannot faithfully represent a whole long document.
Save the vectors (with their text) in a vector index built for fast nearest-neighbour lookup.
At query time, embed the question with the same model and ask the index for the nearest vectors. That is

spans.text: The query must be embedded with the
same model
used for the chunks — otherwise the two sets of points live in different spaces and distance means nothing.

blocks.analogy: Think of a library: chunking is tearing books into single-topic pages, embedding is filing each page by subject, and search is walking straight to the nearest shelf for your question.

blocks.title: How 'closeness' is actually measured

spans.text: Two vectors are compared by an angle, not just a straight-line gap. The most common measure is
cosine similarity
: it looks at the direction each vector points and scores how aligned they are, from -1 (opposite) to 1 (identical direction).
Why direction and not raw distance? Because meaning lives in which way a vector points, not how long it is. Two passages about the same topic point the same way even if one is wordier than the other.
So "nearest neighbour" really means "smallest angle" — the chunks whose direction best matches the query's direction.

blocks.analogy: Cosine similarity is like comparing which way two compass needles point: same heading means same meaning, even if one needle is bigger.

blocks.title: Walk one query through the pipeline

spans.text: "How do I get a refund?" becomes a query vector using the same embedding model the chunks used.
The index computes similarity between the query vector and each stored chunk vector.
The highest-scoring chunks — say the top 5 — are returned as the most relevant passages.

blocks.title: Concrete use case: indexing a product manual

spans.text: A 200-page manual is ingested, split into ~800
chunks
of a few paragraphs each, and every chunk is embedded and stored once.

When a user asks "how do I replace the filter?", the question is embedded and the index instantly returns the three chunks whose vectors point most like the query — the filter-replacement section — without scanning all 800 by hand.

blocks.prompt: What is the correct order of the indexing-and-search pipeline?

options.text: Embed → Ingest → Chunk → Search → Store
Ingest → Chunk → Embed → Store → Search
Search → Chunk → Embed → Ingest → Store

blocks.explanation: You ingest documents, split them into chunks, embed each chunk into a vector, store the vectors, then embed queries and search the store for nearest neighbours.

modules.title: Design choices
modules.sub: Follows the mechanism: the few knobs that decide quality, cost, and latency.
modules.summary: The pipeline has a handful of high-leverage knobs: chunk size, which embedding model, exact vs approximate search, and whether to add a reranker. This module helps you pick the smallest design that meets the need.
objectives: Explain the tradeoff in chunk size between precision and context.
Say when approximate nearest-neighbour search is worth its small accuracy loss.
Decide when a reranker earns its extra cost and latency.

spans.text: Before reading on, predict:
if you make each
chunk
very large, what do you gain and what do you lose at search time?
Four choices shape almost every retrieval system.

items.text: are precise but lose surrounding context; large chunks keep context but dilute the match, so the relevant sentence drowns in noise.
models capture nuance but cost more per call and produce larger vectors to store.
Exact search checks every vector (slow at scale); approximate nearest-neighbour search trades a little accuracy for huge speed.
re-scores the top results with a slower, more accurate model to push the best answer to position one.

spans.text: A common upgrade is hybrid retrieval — run keyword and
vector search
together and merge the two ranked lists with
RRF
so neither blind spot dominates.

blocks.title: Chunk size: drag to feel the tradeoff
blocks.caption: Slide from tiny to huge chunks and read what you win and lose at each setting.

stops.label: Small (a sentence or two)
stops.note: Very precise matches, but a chunk may be missing the context needed to actually answer — you retrieve a fragment.

stops.label: Medium (a paragraph or two)
stops.note: Usually the sweet spot: enough context to be useful, focused enough that the match stays sharp.

stops.label: Large (a whole page)
stops.note: Lots of context, but the one relevant sentence is diluted by surrounding text, so similarity scores blur and precision drops.

blocks.title: How to reason through a design choice

spans.text: Write the user-visible need in one sentence, e.g. "return the right help article in the top 3 results."

steps.label: Pick the smallest design that meets it

spans.text: Start with medium chunks, a standard embedding model, and approximate search. Add a reranker only if the requirement is unmet.
Run a handful of real queries and check whether the right chunk appears in the top results before reaching for heavier machinery.

blocks.title: Which retrieval design fits?

options.name: Pure vector search, approximate

cells.text: Fast even on millions of vectors.

options.whenToUse: Start here: meaning-based search where exact wording varies.

options.name: Hybrid (vector + keyword, RRF merge)

cells.text: Catches exact terms vector search misses (IDs, codes).
Two searches plus a merge step.
Maintain two indexes and fuse with RRF.

options.whenToUse: Use when queries mix natural language with exact tokens like part numbers.

options.name: Vector search + reranker

cells.text: Best top-1 accuracy; reorders the shortlist.
Reranker adds a slower model on the top results.
Add and tune a second model.

options.whenToUse: Use when the single best answer must be first and latency budget allows.

blocks.howToRead: Pick the simplest row that meets your quality requirement; only move down when a measured gap forces it.

blocks.prompt: Why can chunks that are too large hurt retrieval quality?

options.text: Large chunks are always slower to store.
The one relevant sentence is diluted by surrounding text, so the similarity score blurs and precision drops.
Embedding models reject chunks over a fixed size.

blocks.explanation: A vector summarizes the whole chunk. When a chunk mixes many topics, the summary is averaged and the match to a focused query weakens.

modules.decisionItForces: Choose the retrieval design: pure vector search, hybrid with RRF, or vector search plus a reranker.

modules.title: Tiny implementation sketch
modules.sub: Follows the design choices: the smallest runnable embed-store-search loop.
modules.summary: Theory becomes concrete in a few lines: embed the chunks, store them, embed the query, return the top matches. We also cover how to check an AI-generated version before trusting it.
objectives: Read a minimal embed-store-search loop and name each step.
Complete the missing line that ranks results by similarity.
List the specific things to verify in AI-generated retrieval code.

spans.text: A working
vector search
has only three moving parts: a function that turns text into a vector, a place to keep the vectors, and a similarity comparison at query time.
Everything heavier — an index for scale, a
reranker
, monitoring — is added on top of this same shape once you can see it run.

blocks.title: Minimal embed-store-search loop
blocks.code:
import numpy as np

# 1. Embed: each chunk and the query become vectors (model omitted).
chunk_vecs = embed(["payment failed at checkout", "reset my password"])
query_vec = embed(["my card got declined"])[0]

def cosine(a, b):
    return np.dot(a, b) / (np.linalg.norm(a) * np.linalg.norm(b))

# 2. Search: score every stored chunk, return the best match.
scores = [cosine(query_vec, c) for c in chunk_vecs]
best = int(np.argmax(scores))
print("best chunk index:", best)

spans.text: Treat this as the smallest runnable shape: embed the
chunks
and the query, score each chunk with cosine similarity, and pick the highest. A real system swaps the list scan for a vector index, but the logic is identical.

predictThenReveal.prompt: The line `best = int(np.argmax(scores))` is left for you to reason about. Given a list of cosine scores, what does this line return — and why argmax and not argmin?
predictThenReveal.answer: It returns the index of the HIGHEST score. Cosine similarity is larger when two vectors point the same way, so the most similar chunk has the maximum score — hence argmax, not argmin.

syntax.explains: Multiplies the two vectors element-wise and sums — the core of cosine similarity.
Length of a vector; dividing by both lengths isolates direction (angle).
Returns the index of the largest value in the list of scores.

spans.text: If you ask an AI assistant to generate retrieval code, check these four things before trusting it:

items.text: Same model both sides. The query and the chunks must use the identical embedding model, or distances are meaningless.
Normalization matches the metric. If it uses cosine similarity, confirm vectors are normalized (or the formula divides by norms, as above).
It returns the MOST similar. Verify it sorts by highest similarity, not lowest distance flipped the wrong way.
Index is rebuilt when data changes. Confirm new or edited documents are re-embedded, or search will quietly return stale results.

blocks.title: Concrete use case: from sketch to feature

spans.text: The same loop scales up almost unchanged: replace the Python list with a vector index, return the top 5 instead of the top 1, and feed those
chunks
to a language model as evidence — and you have built a basic
RAG
retriever.

blocks.prompt: In the sketch, why is the query embedded with the same model as the chunks?

options.text: To save money on API calls.
Only vectors from the same model share a meaning-space, so distances between them are comparable.
Because the code would not compile otherwise.

blocks.explanation: Different embedding models place text in different spaces. Mixing them makes cosine scores meaningless even if the code runs without error.

modules.title: Check and apply
modules.sub: Follows the implementation: how retrieval breaks, and a go/no-go decision.
modules.summary: Retrieval fails quietly — wrong chunks look like confident answers. This module names the common failure modes, brings back an earlier concept from memory, and ends with a decision and a checklist so the lesson sticks.
objectives: Name three ways a vector search system fails in practice.
Recall the meaning of cosine similarity without looking back.
Decide whether your retrieval is good enough to ship or needs a fix.

spans.text: Before reading on, predict from memory:
in module 2 you learned how closeness is measured. What does cosine similarity compare between two vectors, and what range does it run over?
Answer, then check. (Cosine similarity compares the direction the two vectors point, scoring from -1 for opposite to 1 for identical direction. Same direction means same meaning.)
These failures rarely throw an error — the system returns something, just the wrong something. Watch for each.
1. Bad chunking
Chunks
split mid-sentence or mix several topics. The relevant idea is fragmented or diluted, so the right passage never scores high enough to return.
2. Model mismatch
The query is embedded with a different model than the corpus, or the corpus was re-embedded with a new model but the index was not rebuilt. Distances become noise, and results look random.
3. Stale index
Documents change but their vectors are not re-embedded. Search confidently returns the old version — a silent correctness bug nobody sees until a user complains.
4. Top-1 is wrong (non-obvious)
The right chunk is in the top 10 but not first, so a system that uses only the single best result answers from the wrong passage. This is exactly the gap a
reranker
closes.

blocks.useWhen: Your evaluation queries reliably surface the correct chunk in the top results and the index is rebuilt whenever documents change.
blocks.avoidWhen: The right passage is missing or buried, results shift between runs, or you have never tested retrieval on real queries — shipping now hides a silent correctness bug.
blocks.ruleOfThumb: If a small, fixed set of real queries returns the right chunk in the top few every time, ship it; if not, fix chunking or rebuild the index before adding heavier machinery.

blocks.prompt: A retrieval system suddenly returns seemingly random results after a deploy. Which failure mode is the most likely first suspect?

options.text: The user asked too many questions.
Model mismatch — the query and corpus are no longer embedded by the same model, or the index was not rebuilt.
The vector index is too fast.

blocks.explanation: Random-looking results right after a change almost always mean the query and stored vectors no longer share a meaning-space. Confirm the same model is used on both sides and the index was rebuilt.

modules.decisionItForces: Decide whether your retrieval is good enough to ship or needs a chunking fix or index rebuild first.

rag.label: RAG
rag.laymanDefinition: Retrieving relevant evidence by meaning, then giving it to a language model before it answers.
rag.technicalNote: RAG pairs a vector-search retriever with a generator: the retriever supplies grounded passages so the model answers from evidence rather than memory.

embedding.label: Embedding
embedding.laymanDefinition: A list of numbers that places a piece of text at a point in space, so similar meanings sit close together.
embedding.technicalNote: A fixed-length dense vector produced by a model trained so that semantically related inputs have a high cosine similarity.

vector_search.label: Vector search
vector_search.laymanDefinition: Finding the stored texts whose points are closest in meaning to your query's point.
vector_search.technicalNote: Nearest-neighbour search over embedding vectors using a similarity metric (commonly cosine), often accelerated by an approximate index.

chunk.label: Chunk
chunk.laymanDefinition: A small passage a document is split into before embedding, so each vector covers one focused idea.
chunk.technicalNote: A unit of text (often a few sentences to a couple of paragraphs) embedded and indexed independently; chunk size trades precision against context.

reranker.label: Reranker
reranker.laymanDefinition: A second, slower model that re-scores the top search results to push the single best answer to the top.
reranker.technicalNote: Typically a cross-encoder that jointly scores the query and each candidate chunk for higher top-1 accuracy at the cost of latency.

rrf.label: RRF
rrf.laymanDefinition: A simple rank-based way to merge two result lists (e.g. keyword and vector) into one.
rrf.technicalNote: Reciprocal rank fusion combines rankings by summing 1/(k+rank) across lists, so items ranked high in either list rise to the top.

questions.q: Does your search need to match meaning, not just shared words?
questions.why: Vector search only earns its complexity when phrasing varies between queries and documents.
questions.rot: Prefer the smallest design that returns the right chunk in the top few results.

questions.prompt: Before choosing an answer, try to recall the idea from memory: in this lesson, what is an embedding?

options.text: A number-based representation of text that places similar meanings near each other
A list of exact keywords copied from a document
A database table that stores only full web pages
A prompt template used to make an AI answer in a certain style

questions.explanation: An embedding turns text into numbers so a computer can compare meaning rather than only exact words.

questions.prompt: You are building a retrieval pipeline for product-support docs; which order matches the basic flow?

options.text: Split text into chunks → embed chunks → store vectors → embed the user query → search by similarity
Embed the user query → split the query into chunks → rerank all docs → store keywords → search titles
Store full documents → search exact words → embed only the winner → split the answer into chunks
Rerank chunks → embed documents → delete vectors → search with keywords → split text

questions.explanation: Vector retrieval usually prepares chunks and their embeddings first, then embeds the query and compares it to stored vectors.

questions.prompt: Your search often returns tiny snippets that match the query but lack enough surrounding information to answer well; what design change is most likely to help?

options.text: Use somewhat larger chunks or add overlap so each result carries more context
Make chunks even smaller so every result is more precise
Remove similarity scoring and return random chunks
Use only exact keyword search for all queries

questions.explanation: Chunk size is a tradeoff: smaller chunks can be precise, but larger or overlapping chunks can preserve needed context.

questions.prompt: When is approximate nearest-neighbour search most worth using?

options.text: When you have lots of vectors and need faster search, accepting a small chance of missing the exact closest result
When your dataset is tiny and exact search is already instant
When you want to avoid embedding your documents
When you need the system to ignore semantic similarity and match exact spelling only

questions.explanation: Approximate nearest-neighbour search trades a little accuracy for speed at larger scale.

questions.prompt: In one or two sentences, what should you verify before shipping AI-generated retrieval code?
questions.acceptableAnswer: A good answer mentions checking that text is chunked as intended, the same embedding model/dimensions are used for documents and queries, vectors are stored and searched correctly, similarity ranking is in the right direction, metadata/source IDs are preserved, and results are tested on realistic queries including failure cases.
questions.explanation: Retrieval code can look plausible while failing through wrong chunking, mismatched embeddings, reversed scoring, missing metadata, or untested bad results.
